name: ent
vendor: ent project (LF Projects, started at Facebook)

foundation.via: A series of LF Projects, LLC, donated by Facebook (now Meta)

summary: A Go entity framework from Facebook: describe entities and their edges as Go code, and `go generate` writes a fully typed client for querying and traversing them in SQL databases.
intro: In ent the schema is Go code. Each entity is a type in `ent/schema/` with a `Fields()` method (`field.String("name")`, `field.Int("age").Positive()`) and an `Edges()` method describing relations to other entities, such as `edge.To("cars", Car.Type)` with an inverse `edge.From("owner", User.Type).Ref("cars")`. Running `go generate ./ent` produces a package of plain Go: a client, builders for create, update and delete, typed predicates such as `user.AgeGT(30)`, and query methods for every edge, so `client.Group.Query().QueryUsers().QueryCars().Where(car.Model("Ford")).All(ctx)` walks from groups to users to cars in one call chain, all checked by the compiler. There are no struct tags, no reflection at run time and no `interface{}` query strings.

The generated code talks to MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL and SQLite, with TiDB and CockroachDB in preview and Gremlin as an experimental graph backend. Around it sit hooks and interceptors on mutations and queries, privacy policies that run authorisation rules at the data-access layer, eager loading with `With…()` methods, and extensions that generate a GraphQL server (with gqlgen) or gRPC services from the same schema. Migrations are either automatic, for prototypes, or versioned files planned by Atlas, the schema tool built by ent’s maintainers. The current release is v0.14.6 (March 2026), and commits continued through October 2026.
strengths: Everything is generated and statically typed: renaming a field or edge breaks the build, not production
Relations as a graph, with traversals across edges that read like the data model rather than like joins
Privacy rules, hooks and interceptors give one place for authorisation, auditing and soft deletes
One schema can also generate a GraphQL API, gRPC services and versioned migrations through Atlas
limits: Code generation is part of every change: edit the schema, rerun `go generate`, and commit a large generated package
Still versioned 0.x after seven years, and some dialects (TiDB, CockroachDB, Gremlin) are preview or experimental
Unusual queries fall back to `sql.Selector` modifiers or raw SQL, which lose the typed API
Opinionated: it wants to own the schema and migrations, which fits new services better than an existing database designed elsewhere

story: Ariel Mashraki joined Facebook Connectivity’s team in Tel Aviv around 2018, where Go spread from one project to a group of about 15 engineers. Facebook’s internal teams thought about data as a graph of entities and edges, but Go had no graph-based ORM, so he wrote one. Development started against Gremlin on AWS Neptune and later moved to MySQL. Facebook open-sourced it as ent on 3 October 2019, with the principles “Schema As Code”, a statically typed and explicit API generated by codegen, and simple queries, aggregations and graph traversals.

On 31 August 2021 Facebook moved ent to the Linux Foundation, saying a vendor-neutral home would let its maintainers chart its course; by then engineers from GitHub, Mail.ru, Scaleway and Virta Health had contributed. Mashraki and fellow maintainers founded Ariga to build Atlas, which became ent’s migration engine. Development has slowed to occasional releases, the latest being v0.14.6 in March 2026.

choices.choice: Schema as Go code, not struct tags
choices.why: Types, relations and constraints written in Go can be validated by tools and drive the code generator, instead of hiding in strings.

choices.choice: Generate a typed API rather than reflect at run time
choices.why: Mashraki wrote that `interface{}`-based APIs slow developers down, especially newcomers; generated methods and predicates let the compiler catch mistakes.
Facebook’s teams already thought in entities and edges, so traversals such as user → groups → users map directly to code.
The code generator works from templates, so the same schema could target Gremlin first and SQL databases later.
